q: What is the main purpose of booting a computer?
options: To permanently erase data from the hard disk
To initialise hardware and load the OS kernel into RAM
To install new application software automatically
To connect the computer to the Internet
explain: Booting prepares the machine for use by initialising essential hardware and loading the operating-system kernel into RAM.

q: The word "boot" in computing is derived from which term?
explain: Boot is short for bootstrap, the idea of a system pulling itself up by its own bootstraps.

q: Which of the following shows the correct order of a typical boot sequence?
options: BIOS/UEFI, POST, boot loader, OS kernel, login screen
POST, OS kernel, BIOS/UEFI, boot loader, login screen
Boot loader, BIOS/UEFI, POST, login screen, OS kernel
BIOS/UEFI, boot loader, POST, login screen, OS kernel
explain: Firmware starts first, POST checks hardware, the boot loader loads the kernel, and finally the login screen or desktop appears.

q: In the boot sequence, which program loads the OS kernel into RAM and passes control to it?
explain: The boot loader loads the kernel into RAM and transfers control to it. POST only checks hardware.

q: Which of the following executes first when a computer is switched on?
options: Firmware such as BIOS or UEFI
explain: Firmware runs before the boot loader and the operating system. Ordinary applications load only after the OS.

q: Where is the BIOS/UEFI normally stored?
options: In non-volatile motherboard memory, usually flash
In the RAM of the computer
In the cache memory of the printer
explain: Firmware sits in non-volatile memory on the motherboard (traditionally described as ROM, now commonly flash) so it survives power-off.

q: During booting, which memory holds the kernel and the active OS components?
explain: The installed OS lives on the SSD/HDD, but the kernel and active components are loaded into RAM to run.

q: Which statement is correct?
options: Applications such as Paint load before the OS
The OS is loaded before ordinary applications like Paint
The boot loader runs before the firmware
The kernel is a type of application program
explain: Order is firmware, boot loader, OS, then applications. The kernel is the core of the OS, not an application.

q: Pressing the power button on a computer that has been shut down is called a:
explain: Starting from a powered-off state is a cold boot, also called a cold start or hard boot.

q: Selecting "Restart" from the Start menu of a running computer is an example of:
explain: Restarting without manually switching off the power is a warm boot (warm restart or soft reboot).

q: What is the full form of BIOS?
explain: BIOS stands for Basic Input/Output System, the firmware that initialises hardware and begins startup.

q: UEFI stands for:
explain: UEFI = Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, the modern firmware interface that replaces legacy BIOS.

q: POST in the context of booting means:
explain: POST (Power-On Self-Test) is a set of firmware routines that check essential hardware like memory and devices.

q: Which statement about POST is correct?
options: It is part of the firmware, not a separate hardware device
It is a separate chip fitted on the hard disk
It is a program loaded after the desktop appears
It is a type of boot loader for Linux
explain: POST belongs to the firmware and runs the initial hardware checks at startup.

q: Which file system is normally used for the EFI System Partition on fixed disks?
explain: UEFI startup files are stored in the EFI System Partition, normally formatted as FAT32.

q: Where did traditional PCs retain BIOS settings?
options: Boot sector of the hard disk
explain: Traditional PCs kept settings in battery-backed CMOS; modern firmware may use NVRAM instead.

q: GRUB is a:
options: Boot loader widely used with Linux
explain: GRUB (GRand Unified Bootloader) loads the OS kernel and can show a menu to choose an operating system.

q: Having two operating systems installed on one computer, with the user choosing which one to start, is called:
explain: Dual boot lets the user pick between two installed operating systems at startup.

q: MBR stands for:
explain: The Master Boot Record is a disk structure that traditionally holds initial boot code and partition information.

q: Safe Mode in Windows is mainly used to:
options: Diagnose startup and software problems with limited drivers and services
explain: Safe Mode starts Windows with only essential files, drivers and services so faults can be diagnosed.

q: Which Safe Mode option adds network components?
explain: Safe Mode with Networking loads the network components in addition to the basic Safe Mode set.

q: In modern Windows, what does Ctrl + Alt + Delete normally do?
explain: Historically linked to a warm reboot on older PCs, it now opens the security screen and does not directly restart the PC.

q: Which of the following is NOT a likely cause of sudden, repeated unexpected restarts?
explain: Faulty RAM, overheating and power problems (also malware and bad drivers) can cause unexpected restarts; a monitor size does not.

q: "Random booting" is best described as:
options: A standard type of booting like cold boot
A fault symptom of sudden or repeated unexpected restarts
A boot mode that selects the OS at random
A feature that speeds up startup
explain: Random booting is an informal term for a fault symptom, not a standard boot type.

q: Unicode is best described as a:
explain: Unicode assigns code points to characters of many writing systems. It is neither a font nor a keyboard layout.

q: Work on Unicode began in late:
explain: Unicode work began in late 1987; the Consortium was incorporated in 1991 and the first version came out in October 1991.

q: How many bytes per scalar value does UTF-32 use?
explain: UTF-32 has 32-bit code units and always uses 4 bytes per scalar value.

q: Which Unicode encoding form uses 1 to 4 bytes per scalar value?
explain: UTF-8 uses 8-bit code units, giving 1 to 4 bytes per scalar value.

q: Which statement about Unicode is correct?
options: Unicode is an acronym for a coding standard
Unicode has one fixed length of 16 bits
A font supplies glyph shapes while Unicode identifies characters
explain: Unicode has no single fixed bit length and is not an acronym; fonts draw the glyphs for the characters it identifies.

q: EBCDIC stands for:
options: Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code
Enhanced Binary Computer Data Interchange Code
Extended Basic Coded Digital Information Code
Electronic Binary Coded Decimal Input Code
explain: EBCDIC = Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code, a character encoding like ASCII.

q: ASCII stands for:
options: American Standard Code for Internet Interchange
Asian Standard Code for Information Interchange
American Standard Code for Information Interchange
American Scientific Code for Information Interchange
explain: ASCII is the American Standard Code for Information Interchange.

q: Standard ASCII is a fixed-length code of how many bits?
explain: Standard ASCII uses 7 bits, giving 2^7 = 128 code values (0-127).

q: How many code values are available in Extended ASCII (8-bit)?
explain: With 8 bits there are 2^8 = 256 code values, numbered 0-255.

q: Who contributed a 1961 proposal for a common character code that led to ASCII?
explain: IBM engineer Bob Bemer contributed the 1961 proposal; the first ASCII standard was published in 1963.

q: Which statement about Extended ASCII is correct?
options: It refers to several ASCII-based 8-bit code pages
It is one single universal 8-bit table
It uses 16 bits for each character
explain: Extended ASCII is not one table; the upper-half values (128-255) depend on the code page.

q: What is the ASCII decimal value of the capital letter A?
explain: Uppercase A-Z run from 65 to 90, so A = 65.

q: What is the ASCII decimal value of the lowercase letter a?
explain: Lowercase a-z run from 97 to 122, so a = 97.

q: The ASCII values 48 to 57 represent:
explain: Digits 0-9 occupy 48-57, uppercase A-Z 65-90 and lowercase a-z 97-122.

q: The ASCII value of a lowercase letter is greater than its uppercase letter by:
If the ASCII value of "D" is 68, what is the ASCII value of "d"?
explain: Add 32 to convert uppercase to lowercase: 68 + 32 = 100.
